lead: The two sidebands of DSB-SC are mirror images, so each one alone holds the whole message. Single-sideband modulation (SSB) sends just one of them, halving the bandwidth to W and the power to a quarter of a fully modulated AM carrier's share. It needs a sharp filter or a 90° phase-shift network at the transmitter and a coherent detector at the receiver. Vestigial-sideband modulation (VSB) sends one sideband plus a small slice, the vestige, of the other. It suits messages with energy down to 0 Hz, such as television video.
prereq: You need: DSB-SC and coherent detection from DSB-SC modulation and coherent detection, and the Hilbert transform from Hilbert transform and complex envelope.

blocks.text: Let the message m(t) occupy f<sub>L</sub> to W hertz. DSB-SC puts an upper sideband from f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>L</sub> to f<sub>c</sub> + W and a lower sideband from f<sub>c</sub> − W to f<sub>c</sub> − f<sub>L</sub>. SSB keeps one of them: an upper-sideband (USB) signal or a lower-sideband (LSB) signal, and the name must say which.
W is the highest message frequency in hertz and f<sub>v</sub> the width of the vestige in hertz.

For one test tone, AM at m = 1 radiates 1.5P<sub>c</sub>, DSB-SC radiates the two sidebands, 0.5P<sub>c</sub>, and SSB one sideband, 0.25P<sub>c</sub>. So against full AM, DSB-SC saves 66.7 % and SSB 83.3 % of the power, and SSB also halves the band. SSB serves crowded HF voice links; some syllabi call it SSB-SC.

sections.h3: Making SSB: filter, phase-shift and Weaver methods

blocks.text: Filter method. Make DSB-SC, then a band-pass filter keeps one sideband. Speech has almost nothing below 300 Hz, so the two sidebands are separated by a gap of 2 × 300 = 600 Hz around fc. The filter must pass fully on one side of that gap and reject strongly on the other. Such a narrow transition is practical only at a low carrier, so the sideband is made there and then mixed up to the final frequency.

Phase-shift (Hartley) method. Two product modulators are fed in quadrature. One multiplies m(t) by cos 2πfct. The other multiplies m̂(t) by sin 2πfct, where m̂(t) is the Hilbert transform: every positive-frequency component delayed by 90°, so cos 2πfmt becomes sin 2πfmt. Adding or subtracting the branches cancels one sideband:
the upper sideband; a plus sign gives the lower sideband. The gain A<sub>c</sub>/2 is left out.

For a tone, cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t − sin 2πf<sub>m</sub>t sin 2πf<sub>c</sub>t = cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>)t, one line at f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>. No sharp filter is needed, but the 90° shift must hold across the whole audio band, and any amplitude or phase mismatch between the branches leaves part of the unwanted sideband.

Weaver (third) method. Two quadrature branches mix the message with an audio tone at the band centre, low-pass filter, then mix with the carrier. It needs neither a wideband 90° network nor a sharp filter.

Detection. SSB has no carrier, so it needs a coherent detector. A phase error φ leaves the output amplitude unchanged and shifts the phase of every tone by φ, which the ear hardly notices. A frequency error Δf shifts every tone by Δf: with Δf = 10 Hz, a 1 kHz tone comes out at 1.01 kHz or 0.99 kHz. Speech then sounds high- or low-pitched. This differs from DSB-SC, where the same error gives a beat.

sections.h3: VSB: one sideband plus a vestige

blocks.text: Television video has energy from almost 0 Hz up to several megahertz, so there is no gap between its sidebands and the filter method cannot work. VSB keeps the upper sideband, a vestige of width f<sub>v</sub> of the lower one, and lets the filter roll off gradually through f<sub>c</sub>. In the PAL-B system once used for Indian terrestrial television the video band is 5 MHz and the vestige 0.75 MHz, so the video occupies 5.75 MHz of the 7 MHz channel.

The roll-off must be shaped. After coherent detection, the part of the vestige folded down from below f<sub>c</sub> adds to the part of the upper sideband near f<sub>c</sub>. The message comes out undistorted only if the two filter gains add to a constant:
H is the VSB filter gain and x the distance from the carrier in hertz. The filter is 0.5 at f<sub>c</sub> and its slope is skew-symmetric about f<sub>c</sub>.
Broadcast TV adds a large carrier so that receivers can use an envelope detector. The figure draws the spectra of DSB-SC, USB and VSB for the first worked example.

examples.question: A speech band of 0.3 kHz to 3.4 kHz modulates a 100 kHz carrier. Give the occupied frequencies and bandwidths of DSB-SC, the USB and LSB signals, and VSB with a 0.5 kHz vestige below the carrier. Then compare the radiated powers for a test tone if AM at m = 1 would have a 10 kW carrier.
steps: DSB-SC: LSB 100 − 3.4 = 96.6 kHz to 100 − 0.3 = 99.7 kHz, USB 100.3 kHz to 103.4 kHz; B = 2W = 6.8 kHz.
USB signal: 100.3 kHz to 103.4 kHz. LSB signal: 96.6 kHz to 99.7 kHz. B = W = 3.4 kHz (3.1 kHz of it carries energy).
The gap between the sidebands is 99.7 to 100.3 kHz, 0.6 kHz wide: the filter's whole transition band.
VSB: the channel runs from 100 − 0.5 = 99.5 kHz to 103.4 kHz, B = W + f<sub>v</sub> = 3.4 + 0.5 = 3.9 kHz.
Power: AM P<sub>t</sub> = 10 × (1 + ½) = 15 kW; DSB-SC 10 × ½ = 5 kW; SSB 10 × ¼ = 2.5 kW.
examples.answer: DSB-SC 96.6 to 103.4 kHz (6.8 kHz); USB 100.3 to 103.4 kHz and LSB 96.6 to 99.7 kHz (3.4 kHz); VSB 99.5 to 103.4 kHz (3.9 kHz). Powers 15, 5 and 2.5 kW: SSB saves 83.3 %.

examples.question: A VSB filter has gain rising in a straight line from 0 at f<sub>c</sub> − 0.75 MHz to 1 at f<sub>c</sub> + 0.75 MHz. Find its gain at f<sub>c</sub>, f<sub>c</sub> ± 0.25 MHz and f<sub>c</sub> ± 0.5 MHz, and check the VSB condition.
steps: The line is H(f<sub>c</sub> + x) = 0.5 + x/(2 × 0.75) for |x| ≤ 0.75 MHz.
Every pair adds to 1, so the folded vestige fills in exactly what the upper sideband lost near f<sub>c</sub>.
examples.answer: H = 0.5 at f<sub>c</sub>; 0.667 and 0.333 at ±0.25 MHz; 0.833 and 0.167 at ±0.5 MHz. Each pair sums to 1, so the filter meets the VSB condition.

traps: Writing 'SSB' with no side. Say USB or LSB: the LSB of a 100 kHz carrier is 96.6 to 99.7 kHz, the USB 100.3 to 103.4 kHz.
Saying an SSB frequency error gives a beat. In SSB it shifts every tone by Δf; the beat belongs to DSB-SC.
Taking the VSB bandwidth as 2W or W. It is W + f<sub>v</sub>: 3.4 + 0.5 = 3.9 kHz in the first example.
Calling the Hilbert transform a +90° shift of everything. It delays positive frequencies by 90°: cos becomes sin. The wrong sign gives the other sideband.

quiz.q: Name the three methods of generating SSB.
quiz.a: The filter method, the phase-shift (Hartley) method and the Weaver (third) method.

quiz.q: A 0 to 4 kHz message is sent as SSB on a 50 kHz carrier. Give the USB and LSB bands and the bandwidth.
quiz.a: USB 50 to 54 kHz; LSB 46 to 50 kHz; B = 4 kHz.

quiz.q: A VSB signal has W = 5 MHz and f<sub>v</sub> = 0.75 MHz. Compare its bandwidth with DSB and SSB.
quiz.a: VSB 5.75 MHz; DSB 10 MHz; SSB 5 MHz. VSB saves 4.25 MHz against DSB and costs 0.75 MHz more than SSB.

quiz.q: Show with a tone that the phase-shift method gives a single line.
quiz.a: With m = cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t, m̂ = sin 2πf<sub>m</sub>t: cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t − sin 2πf<sub>m</sub>t sin 2πf<sub>c</sub>t = cos 2π(f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>)t, only the USB line.

quiz.q: An SSB receiver's oscillator is 10 Hz high. What happens to a 1 kHz tone, and why is this different from DSB-SC?
quiz.a: Every tone moves by 10 Hz: 1 kHz comes out at 0.99 or 1.01 kHz depending on the sideband, so speech changes pitch. In DSB-SC both sidebands are present and the error gives m(t) cos 2πΔft, a beat.

quiz.q: Why does VSB, not SSB, suit television video?
quiz.a: Video has energy down to near 0 Hz, so there is no gap between the sidebands for an SSB filter. VSB lets the filter roll off through f<sub>c</sub> and corrects the result with the condition H(f<sub>c</sub> + x) + H(f<sub>c</sub> − x) = 1, using only a little more band than SSB.

beyond: SSB with suppressed carrier remains the voice mode of HF marine, aviation and amateur radio. Digital SSB exciters compute the Hilbert transform in software. The ATSC digital television standard uses 8-VSB, a digital form of vestigial sideband. Search next for Weaver modulator, Hilbert FIR filter and 8-VSB.

figure.caption: Worked example 1, the 0.3 to 3.4 kHz speech band on a 100 kHz carrier. DSB-SC has two mirror-image sidebands with a 0.6 kHz gap at the carrier; the USB signal keeps the upper one (3.4 kHz); VSB keeps it plus a vestige below 100 kHz, with a filter edge (dashed) that is 0.5 at the carrier.
